officialDocs.label: Make your app public and get listed

verdict.summary: Creating an OAuth app takes minutes, but new apps are private to your own Close organization until you click 'Make Public' and Close approves it by email, with no published criteria or timeline. Scopes are all-or-nothing (all.full_access + offline_access), and Close also runs an MCP server with Dynamic Client Registration, which lets MCP-capable agents connect without any app registration at all.

evidence.note: Create the app in Settings, run the code flow against your own organization.

timeToProd.assumes: A REST-API OAuth app made public through Close's review; an agent that speaks MCP can instead connect to mcp.close.com via Dynamic Client Registration the same day.
timeToProd.waitingOn: Close's review of the 'Make Public' request (reply by email, no stated SLA).

evidence.label: inferred
evidence.note: Close publishes no review timeline; the range is our estimate.

verdict.cost: Customers need a paid Close subscription; Close's docs don't mention a fee to publish or list an app.

scopeTiers.impact: Same access as an API key, for the user's chosen organization. There's no way to pick narrower REST scopes; other needs go through Close support. Review is about making the app public, not about scopes.
Read-only tools via the hosted MCP server, with clients registered dynamically.

steps.title: Decide between REST OAuth and MCP
steps.detail: If your agent speaks MCP over HTTP Streamable, it can connect to https://mcp.close.com/mcp with OAuth and Dynamic Client Registration. For a custom REST integration, register your own OAuth app.

steps.title: Create the OAuth app
steps.detail: Go to Settings → Developer → OAuth Apps → Create App. Enter name, description, HTTPS redirect URL, ToS and privacy URLs. Copy the Client ID and Client Secret.

steps.title: Implement the authorization code flow
steps.detail: Send users to https://app.close.com/oauth2/authorize/?client_id=...&response_type=code&redirect_uri=...; they pick an organization. Exchange the code form-encoded at POST https://api.close.com/oauth2/token/. Store organization_id and user_id from the response. PKCE (S256) is advertised.

steps.title: Implement rotating refresh tokens
steps.detail: Access tokens last expires_in seconds (3600 in the example). Each refresh returns a new refresh token and revokes the old one, so persist it atomically.

steps.title: Handle rate limits
steps.detail: Read the RateLimit header (limit, remaining, reset) and sleep for reset seconds on 429. Limits are per endpoint group, per key, and per organization (3× the key limit).

steps.title: Test inside your own organization
steps.detail: Authorize the private app as a member of your organization and confirm API calls such as GET https://api.close.com/api/v1/me/ work.

steps.title: Request to make the app public
steps.detail: In Settings → Developer → OAuth Apps, select the app, click 'Make Public' and submit it for review.

steps.title: Close reviews the app
steps.detail: Close reviews and replies by email. After approval any Close user can authorize the app.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: No criteria or timeline are published.

steps.title: Optional: request an Integrations Directory listing
steps.detail: Draft an email to support@close.com, subject 'Integration Listing Request', with name, description, product link, what it does with Close, and the Client ID. Only after the app is public.

Add RateLimit-header backoff per endpoint group

blockers.symptom: Users outside your organization can't authorize the app
blockers.cause: New OAuth apps are private: only members of your own Close organization can authorize them.
blockers.fix: Click 'Make Public' and wait for Close's approval.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: The exact error shown to outside users wasn't documented.

blockers.symptom: Refresh fails with an invalid token after a previous refresh
blockers.cause: Refresh tokens rotate: the old one is revoked when a new one is issued.
blockers.fix: Persist the new refresh token from every refresh response, and serialize refreshes per connection.

blockers.symptom: No refresh_token in the token response
blockers.fix: Check the app's scopes; new apps get all.full_access offline_access by default.

blockers.symptom: {"error": "invalid_client", "error_description": "The client does not exist on this server."}
blockers.cause: Wrong or deleted client_id, or credentials from a different environment.
blockers.fix: Copy the Client ID and Secret again from the OAuth Apps settings page.

evidence.label: tested
evidence.note: Observed from POST https://api.close.com/oauth2/token/ with bogus credentials on 2026-10-20.

blockers.cause: Per-key or per-organization endpoint-group limit reached; some endpoints may 429 unpredictably.
blockers.fix: Sleep for the RateLimit reset value and spread load across endpoint groups.

blockers.symptom: Redirect URL rejected when creating the app
blockers.fix: Use an HTTPS URL (a tunnel for local development).

nuances.text: REST OAuth apps get all.full_access, the same access as an API key, so there's no least-privilege option for reading data; MCP connections do offer read, write_safe and write_destructive scopes.

api.close.com publishes RFC 8414 authorization server metadata with a registration_endpoint (https://api.close.com/oauth2/register/), PKCE S256 and token auth method 'none', which is what makes DCR-based MCP connections work.

evidence.label: tested
evidence.note: Fetched 2026-10-20. Whether DCR clients can call the REST API outside MCP wasn't tested.

nuances.text: A connection is per user and per organization (the user picks one at consent). Users in several organizations need one connection each.
Rate limits are enforced per endpoint group; the organization-wide limit is 3× the per-key limit, so all integrations in an org compete for the same pool.
There's no OIDC discovery document; this is plain OAuth 2.0 without ID tokens.
